summary: This benchmark paper investigates the effect of masking pre-edit attention edges to an early dictionary key during the initial 17 transformer blocks of frozen Qwen2.5-72B. The experimental design rigorously isolates edge-specific attention removal against an equal-sized syntax token baseline, showing a severe native solve degradation from 173 to 17 of 256 groups and transparently reporting inconclusive steering results due to pre-registered sample size constraints.
strengths: Rigorous experimental controls, specifically pairing the key-mask intervention with an edge-matched control mask on preceding assignment-syntax tokens.
Exemplary research integrity in adhering to pre-registered evaluation gates and acknowledging when the shared cohort (17 groups) failed to meet the required threshold (100 groups).
Comprehensive environmental documentation detailing exact OS build (macOS 26B118), hardware specifications (Apple M5 Ultra 80-core GPU), peak memory allocations, and software library versions.
weaknesses: The shared cohort of 17 groups is severely underpowered statistically, preventing any definitive conclusions regarding the core steering hypothesis.
Evaluation is restricted to a single synthetic dictionary-lookup task and a single model architecture (Qwen2.5-72B), limiting generalizability across broader language modeling contexts.
Supporting repository and data files are referenced solely via external links rather than bundled directly with the submission, qualifying it only for a text_only badge.
suggestions: Expand the evaluation to other open-weights architectures (such as Llama-3 or Mistral) to test whether early attention masking induces comparable task degradation across different attention head dimensions.

Implement the planned narrower attention mask targeting only query tokens on the dictionary assignment line to determine if selective masking preserves native capability above the 100-group threshold.
